source.title: A comparative evaluation and analysis of three generations of Distributional Semantic Models
source.authors: Alessandro Lenci; Magnus Sahlgren; Patrick Jeuniaux; Amaru Cuba Gyllensten; Martina Miliani

record.tranche_reason: The study compares representational geometry across distributional models and reports that alignment varies substantially with word frequency and part of speech, qualifying any broad convergence claim.
record.gate_note: The representational similarity analysis (RSA) results are included because they directly measure similarity between models' semantic spaces. The static-versus-BERT benchmark scores and task evaluations are excluded: they assess task performance, not convergence of representations. The study uses cosine similarities to form representational similarity matrices and Spearman correlation to compare them; it does not compare alternative similarity metrics or test scale.
record.test_reason: The study runs RSA (cosine RSMs compared by Spearman) across 27 language DSMs: count, predict and BERT-derived type vectors. Between-model alignment changes sharply with the frequency and part of speech of the sampled words. This bears on input dependence (V6) and incomplete alignment (V7). There is no scale sweep, no seeds, no mapping and no cross-modal data.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find between-model correlation 'extremely high' for high-frequency words and often dramatically different spaces for low-frequency words. Nouns differ most across models; verbs and adjectives align more. Spaces are unstable even when models share the same corpus and comparable settings. They attribute the divergence to how algorithms handle data sparseness rather than to hyperparameters.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses RSA: cosine-based pairwise lexical similarity matrices are compared with Spearman correlation. It does not apply a scale-based convergence test.
record.method_sensitivity: Representational similarity changes with the frequency range and part of speech of the sampled words.
record.problems: Only one RSA comparison measure is used: cosine within each model's representation and Spearman correlation between similarity matrices. No model scale or capability sweep is reported. Low-frequency RSA excludes LDA because many targets receive identical vectors.

untested.parts: Alternative similarity measures (only cosine plus Spearman RSA is used), neighbour-count settings, and out-of-distribution inputs.
A plateau with scale, and whether shared data or objectives cause the alignment. The static models share one corpus and still diverge, but no causal manipulation is made.
Not tested; there is no size or capability sweep.
Not tested; the study is language-only.
Not tested; no mapping or stitching.
Not tested; no feature or circuit comparison.

missing.what: Model-family pattern: predict models cluster together, RI and LDA are global outliers, and BERT spaces differ from static ones. Contextual models become more similar to static ones at high frequency; GloVe aligns with SVD/predict at high frequency but only with predict models at low frequency.
Static models trained on the same corpus with comparable settings still diverge at low frequency, which bears on the shared-data explanation.

record.verdict_notes: There is no scale or capability variable. BERT (the largest model) is not more aligned with the others, but this is not a scale test. Only one similarity measure is used. The task-benchmark sections (4–5) are not about convergence and are rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No scale sweep or relationship between size, capability, and representational alignment is tested.
No vision-language model pairs or paired images and captions are studied.
The study does not compare independently initialized seeds of the same architecture or measure shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment method is tested.
The study does not identify or compare recurring interpretable features or circuits.
It tests dependence on the input words' frequency and part of speech, but not alternative similarity measures, settings such as neighbour count, or out-of-distribution inputs.

It measures incomplete alignment and variation across frequency and part of speech. It does not test a plateau over scale or establish that shared data or objectives cause alignment instead of a common model of reality.

relationships.condition: Language DSMs; RSA on global, frequency-stratified and POS-stratified word samples
relationships.reason: Mean between-model ρ varies with input words. By frequency band (R1–R4), global is 0.15, high frequency 0.44, medium 0.20 and low 0.17. By POS, high-frequency nouns are 0.53 and medium-frequency nouns 0.28 (R5–R10).
relationships.display_finding: Mean between-model ρ was 0.15 globally, 0.44 for high-frequency words, 0.20 for medium-frequency words and 0.17 for low-frequency words; high- and medium-frequency nouns scored 0.53 and 0.28.

source_check.reason: Sections 6.1–6.3 show substantial input dependence: mean rho is 0.15 globally, 0.44 for high-frequency words, 0.20 for medium-frequency words and 0.17 for low-frequency words; Table 6 also shows POS dependence. Alternative similarity measures and OOD inputs are untested.

relationships.condition: Global, medium- and low-frequency word samples
relationships.reason: Alignment is weak: global mean ρ is 0.15 and low-frequency 0.17 (R1, R3, R4, R8–R10). This holds although the static models were trained on the same corpus with comparable settings.
relationships.display_finding: Mean alignment correlation was 0.15 globally and 0.17 for low-frequency words, despite shared corpora and comparable settings for static models.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Global, medium- and low-frequency word samples
source_check.reason: R1, R3, R4 and R8–R10 establish incomplete alignment. The conclusion explicitly reports divergent spaces despite common corpus data and comparable settings. Plateauing and a causal explanation based on shared training data or objectives are untested.

relationships.reason: For high-frequency words, alignment is much stronger: mean ρ 0.44–0.56, and globally outlying models (RI, LDA) converge too. So how incomplete alignment is depends on the input words (R2, R5–R7).
relationships.display_finding: Mean correlations rose to ρ = 0.44–0.56, with RI and LDA also converging on high-frequency words.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R2 and R5–R7 show stronger alignment, but mean rho of 0.44–0.56 remains substantially incomplete, consistent with V7. These results qualify a claim of uniformly weak alignment, which V7 does not make; they support input dependence under V6.
